title: Mind training
hookLine: short Tibetan slogans, carried in the pocket, meant to go off at the worst moment

cards: A coworker drops the ball, again, and the reply taking shape on the screen gets sharper with every line. By the third paragraph it's a closing argument.
The mind has already decided whose fault it is and is busy building the case. Tibetan Buddhism has tools made for exactly that moment.

Not long meditations: slogans, short enough to remember in the middle of a bad afternoon, built to go off right when the case-building starts. One of them is your line today, and at first it sounds like terrible advice.

teach.b: Lojong is Tibetan for mind training. Tibetan tradition traces it to the Indian teacher Atisha, and says a Tibetan teacher, Geshe Chekawa, set it down as a list of short slogans.

Tonglen, the sending and taking from day seven hundred thirty-nine, belongs to this same training. First, the form. A slogan is memorized and carried, so it surfaces on its own in traffic, in a meeting, at the sink.
The training happens out there, not only on the cushion. Second, your line: drive all blames into one. It sounds like everything is your fault.
That isn't what the teachers mean.
The one is a habit inside us that puts our own comfort at the center of everything, what the tradition calls self-cherishing.
When something goes wrong, look there first: not at yourself as a bad person, but at the reflex already writing the closing argument.
Third, trouble becomes the path. Another slogan, in paraphrase: when hard things happen, turn them into practice. The difficult coworker isn't an interruption of the training.
The difficult coworker is the training. Fourth, gratitude.
One more, in paraphrase: be grateful to everyone. Including, the commentaries say, the people who make life hard, because without them there'd be nothing to train with.
The slogans don't ask anyone to pretend nothing went wrong. They change where the mind points when it does.

how: Tibetan Buddhists who practice lojong often memorize the mind-training slogans, study them with a teacher's commentary, and recall them during daily life, especially in difficult moments.

games.q: a coworker drops the ball and the reply on your screen is getting sharper. going by the lojong slogan, where does the blame go?
o: to yourself, as a bad person.
to the self-cherishing reflex building the case.
games.why: drive all blames into one: the one is self-cherishing. not the coworker, and not you as a bad person.

practice: Choose one of today's three slogans, the one that bothers you a little: drive all blames into one, turn hard things into the path, or be grateful to everyone.

Bring up a recent moment when you were building a case against someone, and hold the slogan up next to it, the way you'd hold a key up to a lock. No need to force a result; just let them sit together.

wordCard.voice: Lojong. Mind training, in Tibetan Buddhism: short slogans, traced by tradition to Atisha, carried into daily life and used right when trouble comes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: drive all blames into one. The one is the reflex, not the person. I'll be here tomorrow.
